newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico phone ad plays on anti-American sentiment.
newsitem.headline: Mexico phone ad plays on anti-American sentiment.

text.p: Desperate to hang onto business after it loses its monopoly next year, Mexico's phone monopoly Telmex is lashing out at Mexicans' traditional enemy -- gringo Americans.

Telmex has launched a massive television advertising campaign featuring an evil-looking gringo speaking bad Spanish with a strong American accent who tells viewers he is coming to Mexico to make money off them.
In a particularly unsubtle stroke, the character is named "Burton Helms" -- a play on the highly unpopular U.S. Helms-Burton Act targeting foreign companies who deal in confiscated Cuban assets.
After telling viewers his lucrative new phone business is long distance "because it's run from Chicago", "Burton Helms" disappears from the screen in a cackle of laughter.
A suave Mexican follows him, assuring viewers in impeccable Spanish that only Telmex's LADA (long-distance) phone brand links all of Mexico together.
The ad is targeted at various private phone consortia who have tapped U.S. partners for an assault on Telmex's monopoly from next year.
The new firms include Alestra, 49 percent owned by AT&T, and Avantel, which groups MCI and Mexican bank Banamex.
What the ad doesn't tell viewers is that Telmex, privatised in December 1990, is partly owned by U.S. company Southwestern Bell and France Telecom.
